note: Every phrase below is filed on Wikipedia's List of proverbial phrases — grouped under proverbs, no different from 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.' But each one carries a named author right in its own entry. If a proverb is supposed to be anonymous folk wisdom worn smooth by oral tradition, these are the cases where the label doesn't quite fit the object.

entries.text: Absolute power corrupts absolutely
entries.author: John Dalberg-Acton, 1st Baron Acton
entries.detail: From a letter to Bishop Mandell Creighton — the fuller line is 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.'

entries.text: All things excellent are as difficult as they are rare
entries.author: Baruch Spinoza
entries.detail: The closing line of the Ethics (1677): 'all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.'

entries.text: An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind
entries.author: Mahatma Gandhi
entries.detail: A 20th-century rebuttal aimed straight at the much older Biblical lex talionis.

entries.text: Better to reign in hell than serve in heaven
entries.author: John Milton
entries.detail: Spoken by Satan in Paradise Lost, Book I.

entries.text: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts
entries.author: Virgil
entries.detail: From the Aeneid's account of the Trojan Horse — 'timeo Danaos et dona ferentes.'

entries.text: Brevity is the soul of wit
entries.author: William Shakespeare
entries.detail: Polonius, in Hamlet — ironically, at length.

entries.text: Civility costs nothing and buys everything
entries.author: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
entries.detail: 18th-century letter-writer and poet.

entries.text: Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise
entries.author: Benjamin Franklin
entries.detail: Poor Richard's Almanack — arguably the single biggest one-man aphorism-to-proverb pipeline in English.

entries.text: He who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know
entries.author: Laozi
entries.detail: The Tao Te Ching turns up three separate times on this 'anonymous' list.

entries.text: Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned
entries.author: William Congreve
entries.detail: The Mourning Bride (1697) — the popular version compresses Congreve's actual couplet.

entries.text: If you steal from one author, it is plagiarism; if you steal from many, it is research
entries.author: Wilson Mizner
entries.detail: American writer and bon vivant, 1876–1933 — a fairly modern coinage for a 'folk' saying.

entries.text: It is like juggling sand
entries.author: Ian Murray
entries.detail: One of the more obscure attributions on the whole list.

entries.text: Keep your powder dry
entries.author: Valentine Blacker
entries.detail: From the poem 'Oliver's Advice,' often shortened from 'trust in God and keep your powder dry.'

entries.text: Men are blind in their own cause
entries.author: Heywood Broun
entries.detail: American journalist, 1888–1939.

entries.text: Money demands care, you abuse it and it disappears
entries.author: Rashida Costa
entries.detail: The most recent and least documented attribution on the list — no wider citation trail beyond the Wikipedia entry itself.

entries.text: Not all those who wander are lost
entries.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
entries.detail: From the poem in The Fellowship of the Ring — about as far from oral folk tradition as an origin gets.

entries.text: Old soldiers never die, they simply fade away
entries.author: a Great War soldiers' song
entries.detail: Popularized decades later by Douglas MacArthur's 1951 farewell address to Congress.

entries.text: Some are more equal than others
entries.author: George Orwell
entries.detail: The closing twist of the Seven Commandments in Animal Farm (1945) — not credited inline on the source list, but unmistakable.

entries.text: The innocent seldom find an uncomfortable pillow
entries.author: William Cowper
entries.detail: English poet, 1731–1800.

entries.text: The law is an ass
entries.author: Charles Dickens
entries.detail: Mr. Bumble's line in Oliver Twist.

entries.text: There are none so blind as those who will not see
entries.author: attributed, unresolved, to either Edmund Burke or George Santayana
entries.detail: Wikipedia's own entry hedges — a proverb-shaped line stuck with two rival named claimants instead of none.

entries.text: Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it
entries.author: George Santayana
entries.detail: A paraphrase of a line from The Life of Reason (1905).

entries.text: Truth is more valuable if it takes you a few years to find it
entries.author: Jules Renard
entries.detail: French author, 1864–1910.

entries.text: Variety is the spice of life
entries.author: William Cowper
entries.detail: From the long poem The Task (1785).

entries.text: When in Rome, do as the Romans do
entries.author: St. Ambrose
entries.detail: Advice reportedly given to Augustine of Hippo about Saturday fasting customs.

entries.text: With great power comes great responsibility
entries.author: often credited to Spider-Man / Marvel Comics
entries.detail: The most 20th-century entry on the whole 'ancient folk wisdom' list — first appears in Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962).
